x.ASV: A Prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling-place In all generations.
x.Darby: A Prayer of Moses, the man ofGod. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations.
x.KJV: A Prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
x.YLT: A Prayer of Moses, the man of God. Lord, a habitation Thou--Thou hast been, To us--in generation and generation,

nt: Moses is speaking as if God were actually a **habitation** or place for the Israelites to live. He means that God has protected the Israelites, just as the walls of a home provide shelter. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have protected us]

As the introduction to this psalm discusses, the pronoun **you** is singular here and throughout the psalm because Moses is addressing Yahweh directly. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Moses is using **in generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in every generation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in every generation] or [throughout all generations]

x.ASV: Before the mountains were brought forth, Or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, Even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
x.Darby: Before the mountains were brought forth, and thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from eternity to eternity thou artGod.
x.KJV: Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
x.YLT: Before mountains were brought forth, And Thou dost form the earth and the world, Even from age unto age Thou art God.

nt: בְּ⁠טֶ֤רֶם ׀ הָ֘רִ֤ים יֻלָּ֗דוּ וַ⁠תְּח֣וֹלֵֽל אֶ֣רֶץ וְ⁠תֵבֵ֑ל

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Consider how you have decided as a translation team to represent Hebrew poetry in your translation, here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Before you created anything at all on the earth]
בְּ⁠טֶ֤רֶם ׀ הָ֘רִ֤ים יֻלָּ֗דוּ וַ⁠תְּח֣וֹלֵֽל אֶ֣רֶץ וְ⁠תֵבֵ֑ל

Moses is speaking as if the **mountains** on earth had actually been **born** and as if God had actually **brought forth**, that is, given birth to, the **earth** and the **world**. He means that God created these things. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Before you created the mountains or formed the earth and the world]

The terms **earth** and **world** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the entire earth]

Moses is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, eternity past and eternity future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout all of time]

As the ULT indicates by using brackets, the verb here is understood, so translators must decide what tense best fits the context. It would be conventional in many languages to use the past tense when describing something that was true a long time ago, so many languages might ordinarily say “you were God.” But Moses means that Yahweh was God long ago, that he is God now, and that he will continue to be God forever into the future. To convey this, the ULT uses the present tense, saying **you are God**. Decide what tense would best convey the meaning in your own language.

x.ASV: Thou turnest man to destruction, And sayest, Return, ye children of men.
x.Darby: Thou makest [mortal] man to return to dust, and sayest, Return, children of men.
x.KJV: Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men.

nt: תָּשֵׁ֣ב אֱ֭נוֹשׁ עַד־דַּכָּ֑א וַ֝⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר שׁ֣וּבוּ בְנֵי־אָדָֽם

Moses is describing one event, **man** returning to **dust**, before describing another event that preceded it, God telling him to do that. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [You say, “Return, sons of man,” and you cause man to return to dust]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people]

Moses is using the expression **return to dust** to mean “die.” It is an allusion to the way that God formed the first man from the dust of the ground, as described in [Genesis 2:7](../../gen/02/07.md). This is one of several mild or poetic ways in which Moses refers to death in this psalm. Your language may have a similar expression that you can use here in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [You cause people to pass away… Pass away] or [You cause people to die … It is time for you to die]

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

x.Darby: For a thousand years, in thy sight, are as yesterday when it is past, and [as] a watch in the night.

x.YLT: For a thousand years in Thine eyes are as yesterday, For it passeth on, yea, a watch by night.

nt: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an affirmation. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

Moses is using the common expression of his culture **in your eyes** to mean “in your perspective.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in your perspective]
כְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶ֭תְמוֹל כִּ֣י יַעֲבֹ֑ר וְ⁠אַשְׁמוּרָ֥ה בַ⁠לָּֽיְלָה

The point of these comparisons is that both of the times that Moses mentions seem very short to people: **the day before**, once it is over, and a **watch in the night** that lasts only a few hours. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [seem very short, like yesterday, when it is over, or like a three-hour watch in the night]

x.ASV: Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep: In the morning they are like grass which groweth up.
x.Darby: Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are [as] a sleep: in the morning they are like grass [that] groweth up:
x.KJV: Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep: in the morning they are like grass which groweth up.
x.YLT: Thou hast inundated them, they are asleep, In the morning as grass he changeth.

nt: The pronoun **them** refers to people, that is, to the “sons of man” whom Moses mentions in verse 3, not to the “thousand years” that he mentions in verse 4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You flood people away]

Moses is speaking as if God actually used a **flood** of water to sweep people **away** from the earth. He is using the image to convey the idea that God may cause people to die suddenly, unexpectedly, and with no recourse. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You bring people’s lives to a swift end]

Moses is speaking as if people were actually **sleep**. This could mean: (1) that Moses is using the term **sleep** as a mild way of referring to death. Alternate translation: [then they are dead] or (2) that Moses is illustrating the brevity of human life by comparing it to **sleep** that lasts only a few hours and then is over. Alternate translation: [their lives are short, like a few hours of sleep that soon end]
The pronoun **it** refers to the life of a human being as compared to grass. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [like grass, a person’s life passes along]

The point of this comparison is that just as grass **passes along** through its brief cycle of life, so human life lasts for only a short time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [A person’s life is short, like grass that quickly passes along]

x.Darby: In the morning it flourisheth and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down and withereth.

Moses says that grass lives for only a single day, lasting only from **morning** to **evening**, as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Grass blossoms and grows for only a short time; very soon it withers and dries up]

The terms **withers** and **dries up** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [it dries up completely]

x.KJV: For we are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled.

nt: Moses is referring to God’s **nose** as a common expression of his culture to mean God’s anger. Your language and culture may also associate anger with a particular part of the body. Alternate translation: [by your wrath we are terrified, and by your anger we perish]

If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. The idea is that God is paying attention to the wrong things that the Israelites have done, and God is punishing them for doing those things, as the previous verse indicates. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You examine our iniquities]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [yes, you have set our hidden sin in the light of your face]

x.ASV: For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: We bring our years to an end as a sigh.
x.Darby: For all our days pass away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a [passing] thought.

nt: Moses is using **our days turn** as a common expression of his culture to describe **days** turning into nights, that is, to describe the light of day fading as evening approaches. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of our days fade away] or [all of our days end]

Moses is using the parts of a lifetime, the **days** of which it consists, to mean an entire lifetime. So in this image, he is speaking of a lifetime that consists of many days as if it were a single day. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our lifetimes fade away] or [our lifetimes end]

In this phrase as well, Moses is using the parts of a lifetime, the **years** of which it consists, to mean an entire lifetime. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our lives end]

The point of this comparison could be: (1) that just as a **sigh** is a brief utterance, so people come to the **end** of their **years** after only a brief time, Alternate translation: [after only a brief time] or (2) that just as someone might **sigh** when they are sad, so we end our lives in despair. Alternate translation: [in sadness]

x.ASV: Return, O Jehovah; how long? And let it repent thee concerning thy servants.
x.Darby: Return, Jehovah: how long? and let it repent thee concerning thy servants.
x.KJV: Return, O Lord, how long? and let it repent thee concerning thy servants.

nt: Moses is using an emphatic imperative form here. It may be appropriate in your culture for someone to address God using an emphatic imperative, and your language may have such a form that you can use in your translation. But if people in your culture would not consider it appropriate for someone to address God in this way, you could translate this as a request rather than as a command. Alternate translation: [Please return, Yahweh.]

This could mean: (1) that Moses wants Yahweh to stop being angry and stop punishing the Israelites. He would be speaking as if Yahweh’s anger were literally a place from which he could **Return**. Alternate translation: [Stop being angry, Yahweh!] (2) that Moses wants Yahweh to abide peacefully among his people, protecting them and blessing them. This would be an allusion to the prayer that Moses always prayed in the wilderness when the cloud of Yahweh stopped moving and the Israelites made camp, as recorded in [Numbers 10:36](../../num/10/36.md), “Return, Yahweh, to the multitudes of the thousands of Israel.” Alternate translation: [Dwell peacefully among us, Yahweh.]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [Until when will you continue to be angry with us] or [For how long will you continue to be angry with us]

Moses is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I hope that your anger will not last long.]

Moses is speaking of himself and his fellow Israelites in the third person as **your servants** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [us, your servants]
